active_paradigms.idea: Exploit incremental cost evaluation with a specialized delta-based local search instead of full-sequence cost recomputation
active_paradigms.description: The current ILS calls workload.get_opt_seq_cost(seq) on the ENTIRE sequence for every candidate move, which is O(n) or worse per evaluation and dominates runtime. Instead, precompute the conflict structure once (which transaction pairs conflict on which keys, and where those conflicting operations sit within each transaction), then implement a delta-evaluation: when swapping two transactions at positions i and j, only the conflicts involving transactions between positions i and j with the moved transactions change. Maintain the cost incrementally so each swap/relocation move evaluation is O(affected-conflicts) instead of O(n). This allows 10-100x more moves per second, meaning the local search reaches far deeper local optima and ILS explores many more basins within the same 113s per workload. The makespan model must be reverse-engineered from txn_simulator/Workload (read the simulator source to understand exactly how get_opt_seq_cost computes makespan - likely a per-transaction start-time simulation where a txn starts after its conflicting predecessors' conflicting ops complete). Build the delta evaluator to mirror that exact semantics, verify it produces identical costs to get_opt_seq_cost on random sequences before trusting it, then run the same ILS loop but with near-free move evaluations.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan on all three workloads by dramatically increasing the number of local-search and ILS iterations within the fixed 360s budget
active_paradigms.cautions: The delta evaluator MUST be validated against workload.get_opt_seq_cost on many random sequences - any mismatch invalidates the search. If the simulator's cost model is too opaque to replicate exactly, fall back to caching full-sequence costs in a dict keyed by tuple(seq) to at least avoid recomputation during plateau walks. Keep the final reported schedule validated with get_opt_seq_cost.

active_paradigms.idea: Reformulate as precedence-constrained sequencing and use a critical-conflict-driven ordering heuristic (insertion-based construction with look-ahead)
active_paradigms.description: Instead of treating the problem as a pure permutation black box, analyze the actual conflict graph: for each key, list the transactions that read/write it. A transaction's completion time is gated by the latest conflicting operation of transactions scheduled before it. Build the schedule incrementally by INSERTION rather than append-only: maintain a partial schedule and repeatedly insert the transaction (at any position) that minimizes the resulting partial makespan, using the simulator's cost function on the partial prefix. This differs fundamentally from the current append-only greedy because a transaction that conflicts heavily with an early transaction can be placed right after it rather than being forced to the end. Combine with a conflict-clustering pre-pass: group transactions that share many hot keys and try to keep conflicting groups contiguous in the permutation (since spreading a conflict group across the sequence forces waiting). Then feed this much better starting solution into the existing ILS refinement. A strong construction reduces the burden on local search and often lands in a better basin than random greedy restarts.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan via better initial solutions and structured neighborhood exploration based on the conflict graph
active_paradigms.cautions: Insertion-based construction is O(n^2) partial-cost evaluations - use partial-sequence costs (prefix only) which are cheaper than full-sequence costs, and cap the candidate insertion positions tried per transaction. Do not rely on heuristics like transaction length alone (the task explicitly warns these do not correlate with makespan); always evaluate with the real cost function.

active_paradigms.idea: Replace ILS with a Lin-Kernighan-style ejection chain neighborhood using a cost cache and adaptive operator pool
active_paradigms.description: The current local search uses isolated pairwise swaps and single relocations, which are weak neighborhoods for sequencing problems - escaping a local optimum requires long coordinated moves. Implement an ejection chain / variable-depth search: remove a transaction from position p1, insert it at p2, which displaces the improvement opportunity to p2's neighborhood, remove the transaction at p2 and try it at p3, and so on, building a chain of up to depth k (e.g., 5-8), accepting the best partial chain prefix found. This single mechanism generalizes swaps, relocations, and 3-opt-like moves. Wrap it in an adaptive operator pool where multiple perturbation operators (segment reversal, random block moves, conflict-pair targeted swaps - swap two transactions that directly conflict on a hot key) are selected with probability proportional to their recent success at producing improvements. Cache all evaluated sequences' costs in a dictionary keyed by tuple(seq) to avoid redundant simulator calls during plateau traversals. Keep the existing time-budget management (113s per call, 339s cap) since it is already well-tuned.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan by escaping local optima that trap the current swap/relocation-only neighborhood, reaching lower-cost basins within the same time budget
active_paradigms.cautions: Ejection chains are more complex to implement correctly - carefully manage the sequence mutation/rollback state at each chain depth to avoid corrupting the sequence. Always fall back to get_opt_seq_cost for final validation of the returned schedule. Limit chain depth and check the deadline frequently inside chain construction so a single long chain cannot consume the whole budget.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use nearly the full 360s evaluation budget by raising the per-workload deadline to ~115 seconds and splitting time adaptively based on workload size
tried_paradigms.description: The evaluator allows 360 seconds total, but the current program hard-codes a 90-second deadline inside get_best_schedule, wasting up to ~90 seconds (25%) of the search budget across the three workloads. Change the deadline logic so that the total available time (measured once at the start of get_random_costs and passed down, or approximated as 115s per workload) is consumed almost fully, leaving a small safety margin for process startup and pickling. Additionally, allocate time proportional to workload difficulty: run a quick greedy on each workload first, and give more time to the workload whose greedy cost is furthest from a quick lower-bound estimate. This is a pure search-budget increase with zero risk — the existing ILS simply gets 25% more iterations, which for a stochastic local search translates directly into better local optima.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan on all three workloads by increasing effective ILS iterations within the 360s evaluator timeout.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Keep at least 10-15s safety margin for Python startup, imports, subprocess overhead, and result pickling, or the run will time out and score 0. Measure time at the very start of the module, not inside get_best_schedule, since the three calls share one process. Verify total runtime stays under 360s on the slowest machine.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace full-sequence cost recomputation with an incremental delta-evaluation of swap and relocation moves using a precomputed conflict/dependency graph
tried_paradigms.description: The bottleneck of the current local search is calling workload.get_opt_seq_cost(seq) on the entire sequence for every candidate move — an O(n) or worse oracle call per move. Instead, precompute the conflict structure: for each pair of transactions, determine which keys conflict and at which operation indices, so that the makespan contribution of a pair depends only on their relative order and the positions of their conflicting operations. Then a swap of two transactions or a relocation only changes the cost contributions involving the moved transactions, so the delta can be computed in O(n) pure Python without touching the oracle. Maintain the full cost incrementally, evaluate thousands of neighborhood moves per oracle call equivalent, and only call get_opt_seq_cost to verify/refresh the incumbent periodically (to avoid drift). This yields orders of magnitude more effective neighborhood exploration within the same wall clock, letting the local search reach much deeper optima.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Search efficiency: number of local-search moves explored per second, leading to lower makespan local optima.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The incremental cost model must exactly match the simulator's cost semantics — study txn_simulator.get_opt_seq_cost carefully first and validate the delta model against the oracle on random sequences before trusting it; refresh the true cost from the oracle whenever a new best is found to correct any accumulated drift. Handle edge cases like transactions with no conflicts and self-conflicts.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: incremental delta evaluation with precomputed conflict graph

tried_paradigms.idea: Large Neighborhood Search with destroy-and-repair (remove a conflicted subset of transactions and greedily reinsert them optimally) instead of blind perturbation
tried_paradigms.description: The current ILS perturbation (segment reversal + random swaps) is unguided and often destroys good structure. Replace it with LNS: in each iteration, select 10-20% of transactions to remove, biased toward transactions involved in the current critical path / largest conflict delays (identifiable by checking which adjacent pairs contribute most to the makespan), then reinsert each removed transaction at its best position via full enumeration of insertion points evaluated with the cost oracle. This keeps the good 80-90% of the schedule intact while optimally repairing the worst parts, which is far more effective than random kicks for scheduling problems. Combine with the existing plateau-accepting local search as a polish step after each repair, and keep the global best. This is the classic LNS paradigm that dominates pure ILS on sequencing problems.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Quality of local optima reached per unit time by making perturbation structure-aware rather than random.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Insertion-point enumeration costs n oracle calls per removed transaction; limit removal size so each LNS iteration stays within a few hundred oracle calls. Bias removal toward transactions on the critical path (those whose conflicts dominate the makespan) rather than uniformly random. Ensure the time deadline check is inside the reinsertion loops so the search never overruns the budget.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: Large Neighborhood Search (destroy-and-repair with greedy optimal reinsertion)
